topics.title: Why Bridges Fail: Forces 101

hook.text: Every bridge on Earth is being pulled apart, crushed, and twisted at the same time.

buildup.text: Tension pulls things apart. Compression pushes them together. Bridges must handle both.

discovery.text: Steel is great in tension. Concrete is great in compression. Engineers use each where it excels.

twist.text: Wind adds a third force: torsion. It twists the bridge. That's what destroyed Tacoma Narrows.

climax.text: Bridge engineering is a constant battle against invisible forces trying to tear the structure apart.

punchline.text: A bridge is a negotiation with gravity.

quiz.question: What three main forces act on every bridge?
options: Friction, magnetism, and vibration
Tension, compression, and torsion
Gravity, buoyancy, and momentum

topics.title: Dead Load vs. Live Load

hook.text: The Golden Gate Bridge weighs 887,000 tons. That weight never changes. But the real danger is what moves.

buildup.text: Dead load is the bridge's own weight — steel, concrete, cables. It's constant and predictable.

discovery.text: Live load is everything that changes — traffic, pedestrians, wind, rain, even temperature expansion.

twist.text: A marching army once collapsed a bridge. Synchronized footsteps created a resonance the structure couldn't handle.

climax.text: Engineers now design for worst-case scenarios: maximum traffic, hurricane winds, and earthquakes combined.

punchline.text: The bridge's weight is safe. It's yours that's dangerous.

quiz.question: What is the difference between dead load and live load on a bridge?
options: Dead load is damage; live load is the original construction weight
Dead load is the bridge's own weight; live load is variable forces
Dead load is underground; live load is above the surface

topics.title: Foundations: What Holds a Bridge Up from Below

hook.text: The Brooklyn Bridge's foundations go 24 meters below the riverbed. Workers dug in pressurized air chambers.

buildup.text: Caissons are watertight boxes sunk to the riverbed. Workers inside excavated mud while air pressure held water out.

discovery.text: Decompression sickness — 'the bends' — crippled workers who surfaced too fast. The cause was unknown in 1870.

twist.text: Chief engineer Washington Roebling got the bends so badly he directed construction from his bedroom with binoculars.

climax.text: Modern foundations use drilled shafts sunk 100 meters into bedrock. No human enters the hole.

punchline.text: Every great bridge starts with a hole in the ground.

quiz.question: What medical condition affected Brooklyn Bridge workers in the caissons?
options: Heatstroke from high temperatures underground
Decompression sickness from surfacing too fast
Lead poisoning from the construction materials

topics.title: Expansion Joints: Letting Bridges Breathe

hook.text: On a hot day, the Golden Gate Bridge is 40 centimeters longer than on a cold day.

buildup.text: Steel expands when heated and contracts when cooled. A 300-meter bridge can grow half a meter in summer.

discovery.text: Expansion joints are intentional gaps in the bridge deck. They let sections slide without cracking.

twist.text: The bump you feel driving onto a bridge? That's the expansion joint. Without it, the road would buckle.

climax.text: Engineers use finger joints, sliding plates, and rubber seals to handle movement while keeping the road smooth.

punchline.text: Bridges grow and shrink. Engineers plan for it.

quiz.question: Why do bridges need expansion joints?
options: To reduce the total weight of the bridge structure
To allow steel to expand and contract with temperature changes
To make the bridge easier to disassemble for repairs

topics.title: Load Paths: How Force Travels Through a Bridge

hook.text: When a truck drives over a bridge, its weight doesn't just push down. It travels a hidden path.

buildup.text: Force flows from the deck to beams, from beams to columns, from columns to foundations, then into the earth.

discovery.text: Engineers trace this load path to find the weakest link. One bad connection can collapse the whole structure.

twist.text: The I-35W bridge in Minneapolis collapsed in 2007. A single gusset plate — 1 centimeter too thin — failed.

climax.text: Every bolt, weld, and joint is part of the load path. Skipping one inspection can be fatal.

punchline.text: Force always finds the weakest link.

quiz.question: What caused the I-35W bridge collapse in Minneapolis?
options: An earthquake exceeded the bridge's design capacity
A single gusset plate was too thin and failed under load
A barge collision damaged the main support column

topics.title: Safety Factors: Engineering for the Unexpected

hook.text: A bridge designed to hold 10 tons is actually built to hold 30. The extra is called the safety factor.

buildup.text: Safety factors account for uncertainties: material defects, construction errors, loads heavier than expected.

discovery.text: Most bridges use a safety factor of 2 to 3. The structure can handle double or triple its rated load.

twist.text: Space engineers use safety factors close to 1.2 because weight is so costly. Every gram counts in orbit.

climax.text: Higher safety factors cost more material and money. Lower ones risk catastrophe. Engineering is a balance.

punchline.text: Build it strong enough. Then triple it.

quiz.question: What does a safety factor of 3 mean for a bridge?
options: The bridge has three backup systems in case one fails
The bridge can handle three times its rated maximum load
The bridge was inspected three times before opening

topics.title: The Beam Bridge: Simplest Span

hook.text: A log across a stream is a beam bridge. It's the oldest and simplest type of bridge.

buildup.text: A beam bridge rests on supports at each end. The beam bends under load — top compressed, bottom stretched.

discovery.text: I-beams use an H-shape to resist bending with less material. The top and bottom flanges do most of the work.

twist.text: Beam bridges can only span about 75 meters before they sag under their own weight.

climax.text: Highway overpasses, footbridges, and most short crossings are beam bridges. Simple, cheap, and effective.

punchline.text: The simplest bridge is still the most common.

quiz.question: What limits the span of a simple beam bridge?
options: Wind forces that push the beam sideways
The beam sags under its own weight beyond about 75 meters
The supports cannot be anchored in deep water

topics.title: Truss Bridges: Triangles Are Unbreakable

hook.text: A square frame collapses if you push it sideways. A triangle holds firm. Trusses exploit this.

buildup.text: A truss bridge uses a web of triangles to distribute forces. Each member handles tension or compression.

discovery.text: Trusses are lightweight yet rigid. A truss bridge uses a fraction of the material a solid beam would need.

twist.text: Covered bridges weren't covered for people. The wooden roof protected the truss from rain and rot.

climax.text: Railroad bridges, crane booms, and even the Eiffel Tower use truss engineering. Triangles are everywhere.

punchline.text: The triangle: geometry's strongest shape.

quiz.question: Why are triangles stronger than squares in structural engineering?
options: Triangles distribute weight evenly to all three corners
A triangle cannot be deformed without changing a member's length
Triangles use less material than any other geometric shape

topics.title: Arch Bridges: Pushing Sideways to Stay Up

hook.text: The Pont du Gard in France has carried water and traffic for 2,000 years. It's a stone arch bridge.

buildup.text: Arch bridges convert vertical loads into horizontal thrust. The arch pushes outward against its supports.

discovery.text: Stone and concrete are perfect for arches because they excel in compression. No steel needed.

twist.text: During construction, arches need temporary wooden frames called centering. Remove them too early and everything falls.

climax.text: Modern arch bridges span over 500 meters. China's Beipanjiang bridge arches across a 565-meter canyon.

punchline.text: The arch doesn't fight gravity. It redirects it.

quiz.question: How does an arch bridge handle vertical loads?
options: It absorbs them into flexible cables above the deck
It converts them into horizontal thrust against supports
It transfers them directly to the riverbed below

topics.title: Cantilever Bridges: Balanced on a Pivot

hook.text: Hold your arm straight out. Your shoulder is the fulcrum. Your arm is a cantilever.

buildup.text: Cantilever bridges extend beams from piers without support underneath. Two arms reach toward each other.

discovery.text: A counterweight or anchor on the landward side balances the extending span. It works like a seesaw.

twist.text: The Quebec Bridge collapsed twice during construction — in 1907 and 1916. 88 workers died the first time.

climax.text: The Forth Bridge in Scotland, built in 1890, still carries 200 trains daily. Cantilevers can last centuries.

punchline.text: Reach out from both sides. Meet in the middle.

quiz.question: How does a cantilever bridge stay balanced?
options: Cables from above pull the extending arms upward
A counterweight on the landward side balances the span
Underwater anchors hold the bridge from below

topics.title: Box Girder Bridges: The Hollow Giant

hook.text: A solid steel beam is strong but heavy. Make it hollow, and it's almost as strong but half the weight.

buildup.text: Box girder bridges use hollow rectangular sections. The closed shape resists twisting far better than an I-beam.

discovery.text: The hollow interior can house utilities — pipes, cables, even walkways for inspectors.

twist.text: In 1970, four box girder bridges collapsed during construction. Thin steel plates buckled under compression.

climax.text: The Mersey Gateway in England uses a box girder that weighs 20,000 tons and spans over 1,000 meters.

punchline.text: Hollow is smarter than solid.

quiz.question: Why are box girder bridges preferred over I-beam bridges for long spans?
options: They look more attractive from the water below
Their closed shape resists twisting much better than open sections
They use more material but require less maintenance

topics.title: Cable-Stayed vs. Suspension Bridges

hook.text: They both use cables and towers. But one drapes a main cable between towers; the other fans cables from them.

buildup.text: Suspension bridges hang the deck from vertical cables attached to massive draped main cables.

discovery.text: Cable-stayed bridges connect cables directly from towers to the deck. No main cable needed.

twist.text: Cable-stayed bridges are faster and cheaper to build. They need smaller foundations and fewer cables.

climax.text: Most new long-span bridges are cable-stayed. Suspension bridges dominate only at extreme lengths.

punchline.text: Same idea, different geometry, different economics.

quiz.question: How do cable-stayed bridges differ from suspension bridges?
options: Cable-stayed bridges use no towers at all
Cables run directly from the tower to the deck with no main cable
Cable-stayed bridges can only be built over water

topics.title: The Suspension Bridge: Spanning the Impossible

hook.text: The Akashi Kaikyo Bridge in Japan spans 1,991 meters — nearly two kilometers of hanging roadway.

buildup.text: Two massive cables drape between towers. Vertical suspender cables hang the deck from the main cables.

discovery.text: The main cables are not single wires. They're bundles of 36,830 individual strands spun together on site.

twist.text: During construction, an earthquake struck. Engineers had to adjust the design while the bridge was partially built.

climax.text: The bridge withstands typhoons, earthquakes, and 23,000 vehicles daily. It was designed for all of them.

punchline.text: Two cables, 36,830 strands. That's how you cross the sea.

quiz.question: How many individual strands make up each main cable of the Akashi Kaikyo Bridge?
options: About 500 thick steel ropes woven together
Exactly 36,830 individual strands spun together on site
A single solid cable forged in a factory and shipped

topics.title: Anchorages: Where the Cable Meets the Earth

hook.text: The Golden Gate's cables pull on their anchorages with 63 million pounds of force. Something has to hold.

buildup.text: Anchorages are massive concrete blocks buried deep in rock. They absorb all the cable tension.

discovery.text: Each anchorage weighs tens of thousands of tons. Their mass alone keeps the cables from pulling free.

twist.text: Some bridges use gravity anchorages on land. Others drill cables into bedrock when there's no room for mass.

climax.text: Without anchorages, the cables would rip free and the entire bridge would snap like a rubber band.

punchline.text: The cables are beautiful. The anchorages do the work.

quiz.question: What is the primary function of anchorages on a suspension bridge?
options: They support the weight of the towers during construction
They absorb the massive pulling force from the main cables
They prevent the bridge deck from swaying in the wind

topics.title: Tacoma Narrows: The Bridge That Danced to Death

hook.text: On November 7, 1940, a bridge in Washington State started twisting in 40 mph wind. Then it tore apart.

buildup.text: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge had a shallow, plate-like deck. Wind flowed over it like an airplane wing.

discovery.text: Aeroelastic flutter caused the deck to twist in a self-amplifying cycle. Each twist made the next one worse.

twist.text: Engineers knew the bridge swayed in wind. They called it 'Galloping Gertie.' Nobody expected it to collapse.

climax.text: After Tacoma Narrows, every suspension bridge is wind-tunnel tested. The failure changed engineering forever.

punchline.text: The wind didn't blow it down. It shook it apart.

quiz.question: What phenomenon destroyed the Tacoma Narrows Bridge?
options: A resonance caused by marching soldiers crossing it
Aeroelastic flutter from wind creating self-amplifying twists
Foundation failure from unexpected flooding underneath

topics.title: Wind Engineering: Taming the Invisible Enemy

hook.text: The Great Belt Bridge in Denmark was designed to resist winds of 250 km/h. It opened in 1998.

buildup.text: Modern bridge decks use aerodynamic profiles — streamlined shapes that let wind pass through, not push against.

discovery.text: Wind tunnel tests use scale models to study airflow. Smoke trails reveal how air moves around the deck.

twist.text: Some bridges have tuned mass dampers — heavy pendulums inside towers that swing opposite to the wind's force.

climax.text: Computational fluid dynamics now simulates millions of wind scenarios before a single bolt is placed.

punchline.text: You can't stop the wind. But you can design around it.

quiz.question: How do tuned mass dampers protect bridges from wind?
options: They block wind from reaching the bridge deck surface
Heavy pendulums swing opposite to the wind's force to cancel motion
They vibrate at high frequency to stiffen the structure

topics.title: Cable Corrosion: The Silent Killer

hook.text: The Williamsburg Bridge in New York lost 40% of its cable strength before anyone noticed.

buildup.text: Water seeps into cable wrapping, reaches the steel wires inside, and rusts them from within.

discovery.text: Engineers can't see inside cables without unwrapping them. Inspections require cutting open the protective cover.

twist.text: Acoustic monitoring now detects wire snaps inside cables. Each broken wire makes a distinct sound.

climax.text: Dehumidification systems pump dry air through cables to prevent moisture. Prevention beats repair.

punchline.text: The most dangerous damage is the kind you can't see.

quiz.question: How do engineers now detect broken wires inside suspension bridge cables?
options: X-ray machines scan the full length of every cable
Acoustic sensors detect the distinct sound each wire makes when it snaps
Drones fly alongside cables and photograph surface cracks

topics.title: The Akashi Kaikyo: World's Longest Span

hook.text: Japan's Akashi Kaikyo Bridge spans nearly two kilometers of open water between Kobe and Awaji Island.

buildup.text: Each cable contains 36,830 strands of wire. Laid end to end, the wire would circle the Earth seven times.

discovery.text: During construction, the 1995 Kobe earthquake shifted the towers one meter apart. Engineers redesigned mid-build.

twist.text: Wind tunnel tests used a 40-meter model. The deck has slots that let wind pass through instead of pushing it.

climax.text: The bridge opened in 1998 and handles typhoons and earthquakes. Its design set the standard for long spans.

punchline.text: Nature tried to stop this bridge. Engineering adapted.

quiz.question: What happened to the Akashi Kaikyo Bridge during the 1995 Kobe earthquake?
options: Both main towers collapsed and had to be rebuilt entirely
The towers shifted one meter apart, forcing a redesign
The cables snapped and the deck fell into the strait

topics.title: The Golden Gate: An American Icon

hook.text: When the Golden Gate Bridge was proposed in 1916, critics said it was impossible. The bay was too wide and too windy.

buildup.text: Joseph Strauss designed a hybrid cantilever-suspension bridge. Then Irving Morrow chose International Orange paint.

discovery.text: The bridge's main cables contain 80,000 miles of wire — enough to circle the Earth three times.

twist.text: A safety net below the deck saved 19 workers' lives during construction. They called themselves the Half-Way-to-Hell Club.

climax.text: The bridge opened in 1937 and is still painted constantly. When painters reach one end, they start over.

punchline.text: They never stop painting the Golden Gate Bridge.

quiz.question: What was unusual about the safety net used during Golden Gate Bridge construction?
options: It was the first time a safety net was used on a bridge project and saved 19 lives
It was made of recycled fishing nets from the bay
It was only installed after 10 workers had already fallen

topics.title: Tower Bridge: London's Moving Marvel

hook.text: Tower Bridge opens about 800 times a year. Each opening takes just five minutes.

buildup.text: Two bascule leaves — 1,100 tons each — pivot on massive bearings to let tall ships pass through.

discovery.text: Originally powered by steam-driven hydraulics, the system now uses electric motors installed in 1976.

twist.text: Tourists often confuse Tower Bridge with London Bridge. The actual London Bridge is a plain concrete span.

climax.text: In 1952, a double-decker bus jumped the gap as the bridge opened unexpectedly. The driver got a medal.

punchline.text: London's famous bridge isn't London Bridge.

quiz.question: How is Tower Bridge commonly confused by tourists?
options: They think it was built by the Romans centuries ago
They mistake it for London Bridge, which is actually a plain span
They believe it connects England to France across the Channel

topics.title: The Brooklyn Bridge: Steel and Sacrifice

hook.text: The Brooklyn Bridge took 14 years to build. Its designer died before construction began.

buildup.text: John Roebling designed it, then died from an infection after a ferry crushed his foot at the site.

discovery.text: His son Washington took over but was paralyzed by caisson disease. His wife Emily managed construction.

twist.text: Emily Roebling studied engineering on her own to communicate between her husband and the builders.

climax.text: When the bridge opened in 1883, Emily was the first person to cross it. She carried a rooster for luck.

punchline.text: Three Roeblings. One bridge. Two tragedies.

quiz.question: Who actually managed the Brooklyn Bridge construction after Washington Roebling was incapacitated?
options: A committee of city engineers took over all duties
His wife Emily Roebling, who taught herself engineering
His brother-in-law, who had a civil engineering degree

topics.title: The Millau Viaduct: World's Tallest Bridge

hook.text: The Millau Viaduct in France stands 343 meters tall — higher than the Eiffel Tower.

buildup.text: Norman Foster designed it to look like a sail floating above the valley. The deck weighs 36,000 tons.

discovery.text: The deck was built on land and pushed out over the valley using GPS-guided hydraulic rams — millimeter by millimeter.

twist.text: Construction was so precise that seven cable-stayed masts were aligned to within 5 millimeters over 2.5 kilometers.

climax.text: Cars drive through clouds on the viaduct. It reduced travel time between Paris and the south by hours.

punchline.text: Taller than the Eiffel Tower. And you drive on it.

quiz.question: How was the Millau Viaduct's deck constructed?
options: Built on land and pushed out over the valley with hydraulic rams
Assembled in midair by helicopters lifting each section
Poured in place using massive suspended forms

topics.title: The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge: Longest on Earth

hook.text: China's Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge is 164 kilometers long. It would take over two hours to walk across.

buildup.text: The bridge carries a high-speed rail line across rice paddies, rivers, and lakes between Shanghai and Nanjing.

discovery.text: 10,000 workers built it in just four years using 450,000 tons of steel and 2.3 million cubic meters of concrete.

twist.text: It's not one bridge — it's thousands of connected spans. Each span is an independent structural unit.

climax.text: Building it elevated solved a problem: it avoids land acquisition disputes across 164 km of farmland.

punchline.text: When you can't buy the land, build above it.

quiz.question: Why was the Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge built as an elevated structure?
options: To avoid flooding from nearby rivers and lakes
To bypass land acquisition disputes across 164 km of farmland
To allow agricultural vehicles to pass underneath

topics.title: The Øresund Bridge-Tunnel: Two Countries, One Link

hook.text: The Øresund link between Denmark and Sweden is half bridge, half tunnel. It disappears into the sea.

buildup.text: A cable-stayed bridge runs 8 km from Sweden, then connects to a 4 km tunnel via an artificial island.

discovery.text: The tunnel protects air traffic. Copenhagen's airport runway is nearby, and a tall bridge would block flight paths.

twist.text: The artificial island — Peberholm — was never landscaped. Nature colonized it. Rare species now thrive there.

climax.text: 15,000 commuters cross daily. Two countries became one job market overnight.

punchline.text: Half bridge, half tunnel, one connection.

quiz.question: Why does the Øresund link transition from a bridge to a tunnel?
options: The seabed is too soft to support bridge foundations in that area
A tall bridge would interfere with Copenhagen Airport flight paths
Danish law prohibited bridges longer than 8 km for safety reasons

topics.title: Self-Healing Concrete for Bridges

hook.text: Concrete cracks. It always has. But what if it could fix itself like skin healing a cut?

buildup.text: Researchers embed bacteria or capsules of healing agents in concrete. When cracks form, the agents activate.

discovery.text: Bacillus bacteria produce limestone when exposed to water and air through cracks. They literally fill the gap.

twist.text: The bacteria can survive dormant inside concrete for up to 200 years, waiting for a crack to appear.

climax.text: Self-healing concrete could save billions in bridge maintenance. The Netherlands is testing it on real structures.

punchline.text: Living concrete. It heals its own wounds.

quiz.question: How do bacteria help self-healing concrete repair cracks?
options: They eat away damaged material to reveal fresh layers
They produce limestone when exposed to water through cracks
They release gas that expands to fill gaps mechanically

topics.title: 3D-Printed Bridges

hook.text: In 2021, a steel pedestrian bridge was 3D-printed and installed over a canal in Amsterdam.

buildup.text: Robotic arms deposited molten steel layer by layer, guided by algorithms that optimized the shape for strength.

discovery.text: The algorithm placed material only where stress required it. The result looks organic, like a metal skeleton.

twist.text: The bridge has embedded sensors. It monitors its own stress, vibration, and temperature in real time.

climax.text: 3D printing could build bridges in remote areas using local materials, no heavy equipment required.

punchline.text: A robot printed a bridge. The bridge watches itself.

quiz.question: What is unique about Amsterdam's 3D-printed steel bridge?
options: It was printed from recycled plastic instead of metal
It has embedded sensors that monitor its own structural health
It was assembled by drones flying above the canal

topics.title: Fiber-Reinforced Polymer Bridges

hook.text: A bridge in Aberfeldy, Scotland, is made entirely of plastic. It opened in 1992 and still stands.

buildup.text: Fiber-reinforced polymers combine glass or carbon fibers with plastic resin. Stronger than steel, lighter too.

discovery.text: FRP doesn't rust, doesn't corrode in salt, and weighs a quarter of steel. Perfect for coastal bridges.

twist.text: FRP costs more upfront, but maintenance savings pay for it in under a decade. Steel bridges need constant repainting.

climax.text: The US military uses FRP for temporary bridges. Soldiers can carry and assemble them in hours.

punchline.text: Lighter than steel. Stronger than rust.

quiz.question: Why is FRP ideal for bridges in coastal environments?
options: It absorbs wave energy and reduces bridge sway
It doesn't rust or corrode in salt and weighs much less than steel
It floats if a section breaks free, preventing debris hazards

topics.title: Smart Bridges: Structures That Talk

hook.text: The Commodore Barry Bridge in Pennsylvania has 700 sensors. It knows when it's stressed.

buildup.text: Strain gauges, accelerometers, and thermometers feed data to computers 24 hours a day.

discovery.text: AI algorithms spot patterns humans miss. A tiny vibration change can signal a crack forming deep inside steel.

twist.text: The US has 617,000 bridges. About 42,000 are rated structurally deficient. Sensors could catch problems earlier.

climax.text: Digital twins — virtual replicas — let engineers simulate aging, weather, and traffic on a bridge that doesn't exist yet.

punchline.text: The safest bridge is the one that tells you it hurts.

quiz.question: How many US bridges are rated structurally deficient?
options: About 5,000 out of 200,000 total bridges
About 42,000 out of 617,000 total bridges
About 100,000 out of 1 million total bridges

topics.title: Living Root Bridges: Nature as Engineer

hook.text: In Meghalaya, India, bridges grow. They're made of living tree roots trained across rivers over decades.

buildup.text: The Khasi people guide Ficus elastica roots through hollow betel nut trunks toward the opposite bank.

discovery.text: After 15 to 30 years, roots interlock and thicken. The bridge strengthens with age — the opposite of steel.

twist.text: Some living root bridges are 500 years old and can support 50 people at once. They outlast any steel bridge.

climax.text: Researchers are studying bio-engineering to grow structures. Nature solved problems we're still working on.

punchline.text: The best bridge doesn't decay. It grows.

quiz.question: How do living root bridges differ from conventional bridges over time?
options: They slowly dissolve and must be regrown every decade
They get stronger with age instead of weakening like steel
They only work in tropical climates near the equator

topics.title: Floating Bridges: Roads on Water

hook.text: Seattle's SR 520 bridge floats on Lake Washington. It doesn't touch the lakebed at all.

buildup.text: Pontoon bridges use hollow concrete boxes that displace water. Buoyancy supports the roadway above.

discovery.text: Norway plans a floating tunnel under the Sognefjord. It would hang suspended in water 1,200 meters deep.

twist.text: Waves, currents, and storms all try to move floating bridges. Anchors and mooring cables hold them steady.

climax.text: Floating bridges cost less than deep-water foundations. Where bedrock is too far down, floating wins.

punchline.text: When the bottom is too deep, the answer is to stay on top.

quiz.question: Why are floating bridges used instead of conventional ones in some locations?
options: They are always cheaper regardless of water depth
They avoid the need for foundations in very deep water
They are temporary and can be removed after a few years
